text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: Who is likely to test your patience today, and how would you treat them if you saw their fault as ignorance rather than malice?
context: Marcus wrote much of the Meditations on military campaign along the Danube. This morning exercise prepares for difficult people in advance, and reframes their behavior as a failure of understanding, not an attack.

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul, particularly when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is immediately in perfect tranquillity; and I affirm that tranquillity is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: What place or moment are you waiting for to feel at peace, and what would it take to find some of that quiet here, today?
context: Marcus owned palaces and country estates, yet argued that the only retreat always available is a well-ordered mind. Later readers called this idea the "inner citadel".

text: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: What harm are you still carrying that lives mostly in the story you tell yourself about it?
context: A core Stoic teaching, inherited from Epictetus: events themselves are neutral, and the injury lies in our judgment of them. Marcus is not denying pain, only the added layer of "I have been wronged".

text: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: What good thing have you been postponing as if you had ten thousand years?
context: Marcus reigned through the Antonine Plague and buried most of his children. Remembering death (memento mori) was, for him, not morbid but a spur to act well now.

text: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it. Unhappy am I because this has happened to me? Not so, but happy am I, though this has happened to me, because I continue free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor fearing the future.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: What keeps breaking against you right now, and what part of you is still standing?
context: The key move is from "because" to "though": misfortune happens, but it cannot stop a person from being just, patient, or honest. The rest of the passage argues that only that inner loss would be real misfortune.

text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,—I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world? Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: Which part of today are you resisting, and how would it look if you saw it as the work you exist to do?
context: Even a Roman emperor struggled to get out of bed. Marcus answers his own reluctance not with discipline for its own sake, but by reminding himself what a human being is for.

text: But so far as some men make themselves obstacles to my proper acts, man becomes to me one of the things which are indifferent, no less than the sun or wind or a wild beast. Now it is true that these may impede my action, but they are no impediments to my affects and disposition, which have the power of acting conditionally and changing: for the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid; and so that which is a hindrance is made a furtherance to an act; and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: What are you currently treating as an obstacle that could be the path itself?
context: The source of the modern phrase "the obstacle is the way". "Acting conditionally" refers to the Stoic reserve clause: pursue your aim, but hold it as "if nothing prevents me", so a blocked plan becomes material for a new one.

text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: Where have you been looking outside yourself for something only you can supply?
context: For the Stoics the only true good is character, which no one can give or take away. Marcus reminds himself that it is not found, but dug for, through daily effort.

text: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee: but on every occasion ask thyself, What is there in this which is intolerable and past bearing? for thou wilt be ashamed to confess. In the next place remember that neither the future nor the past pains thee, but only the present.
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: Take the thing weighing on you most: what part of it, in this exact moment, is actually unbearable?
context: A practical technique: shrink a burden down to the present moment, where it is usually small enough to carry. Anxiety borrows weight from a future that has not arrived.

text: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now. But if anything in thy own disposition gives thee pain, who hinders thee from correcting thy opinion? And even if thou art pained because thou art not doing some particular thing which seems to thee to be right, why dost thou not rather act than complain?
author: Marcus Aurelius
question: What are you complaining about that you could simply act on instead?
context: Marcus walks through each kind of distress and finds a response within reach: revise the judgment, correct the habit, or take the action. Complaint is the one option he rules out.

text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, turning from a thing; and in a word, whatever are our acts. Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts. And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint or hindrance; but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others.
author: Epictetus
question: What did you try to control today that was never yours to control?
context: The opening lines of the Encheiridion, the handbook compiled by his student Arrian. This division between what is up to us and what is not underpins all later Stoic practice. Epictetus was born a slave, which gives weight to his claim that the inner life cannot be owned by anyone else.

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing. When then we are impeded, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves—that is, our opinions. It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.
author: Epictetus
question: Who are you blaming right now, yourself included, for something your own view of it has made worse?
context: The closing lines describe three stages of progress: the beginner blames others, the student blames himself, and the one who has finished learning blames no one. Socrates, who faced his execution calmly, is the proof that death itself is not the terrible thing.

text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will. And add this reflection on the occasion of everything that happens; for you will find it an impediment to something else, but not to yourself.
author: Epictetus
question: What limitation are you facing that restricts your circumstances but not the person you choose to be?
context: Epictetus was lame, by some accounts from mistreatment while enslaved, so the example is his own. "Will" here means the faculty of choice, the one thing he held no illness or master could reach.

text: Begin then from little things. Is the oil spilled? Is a little wine stolen? Say on the occasion, at such price is sold freedom from perturbation; at such price is sold tranquillity, but nothing is got for nothing.
author: Epictetus
question: What small irritation today could you let go of as the price of your own calm?
context: Stoic training starts small. Epictetus frames each minor loss as a transaction: a little spilled oil is the price paid for peace of mind, and a bargain at that.

text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it. Suppose that it is not yet come to you. Do not send your desire forward to it, but wait till it is opposite to you.
author: Epictetus
question: What are you reaching for before it has come to you?
context: At a Roman dinner, dishes were carried around the table. Epictetus uses the image to teach patience and grace: take what is offered, let pass what passes, and do not send your desire ahead of you.

text: You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer. Take care then when you observe a man honored before others or possessed of great power or highly esteemed for any reason, not to suppose him happy, and be not carried away by the appearance. For if the nature of the good is in our power, neither envy nor jealousy will have a place in us.
author: Epictetus
question: Which contest are you in right now whose outcome was never yours to decide?
context: Invincibility here does not mean winning every fight, but entering only the ones decided by your own choices. Once the good is placed there, other people's status stops being a threat and envy has nothing to feed on.

text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you. Therefore especially try not to be carried away by the appearance. For if you once gain time and delay, you will more easily master yourself.
author: Epictetus
question: Who irritated you recently, and what opinion of yours did the actual irritating?
context: Epictetus separates the act, a harsh word or even a blow, from the judgment "I have been insulted." His practical advice is time: a short delay lets reason catch up with the first reaction.

text: If you desire philosophy, prepare yourself from the beginning to be ridiculed, to expect that many will sneer at you, and say, He has all at once returned to us as a philosopher; and whence does he get this supercilious look for us? Do you not show a supercilious look; but hold on to the things which seem to you best as one appointed by God to this station. And remember that if you abide in the same principles, these men who first ridiculed will afterwards admire you; but if you shall have been overpowered by them, you will bring on yourself double ridicule.
author: Epictetus
question: What change are you holding back from because of what others might say?
context: Epictetus warns his students that taking a new way of life seriously invites mockery from old friends. His advice cuts both ways: do not put on airs, and do not give up.

text: If it should ever happen to you to be turned to externals in order to please some person, you must know that you have lost your purpose in life. Be satisfied then in everything with being a philosopher; and if you wish to seem also to any person to be a philosopher, appear so to yourself, and you will be able to do this.
author: Epictetus
question: What have you done lately mainly to be seen a certain way by someone else?
context: A short warning against performing virtue for an audience. For Epictetus, "philosopher" meant someone living by their principles, and the only approval that matters for that is your own.

text: We may learn the wish (will) of nature from the things in which we do not differ from one another: for instance, when your neighbor’s slave has broken his cup, or anything else, we are ready to say forthwith, that it is one of the things which happen. You must know then that when your cup also is broken, you ought to think as you did when your neighbor’s cup was broken. Transfer this reflection to greater things also.
author: Epictetus
question: What misfortune of your own would you call "just one of those things" if it had happened to a friend?
context: A test of perspective: we stay calm about a neighbor's broken cup and are upset by our own. Epictetus asks us to judge our losses with the same even eye we use for other people's.

text: His course will not be straightforward; he must go upwards and downwards, be tossed about, and guide his vessel through troubled waters: he must make his way in spite of fortune: he will meet with much that is hard which he must soften, much that is rough that he must make smooth. Fire tries gold, misfortune tries brave men.
author: Seneca
question: What hardship are you facing right now that is showing you what you are made of?
context: Of Providence answers the old question of why bad things happen to good people. Seneca's reply is that hardship is where character is formed and revealed, as fire proves the purity of gold.

text: We are made angry by some things which we learn at second-hand, and by some which we ourselves hear or see. Now, we ought to be slow to believe what is told us. Many tell lies in order to deceive us, and many because they are themselves deceived.
author: Seneca
question: What are you upset about that you only know second-hand and have not yet checked?
context: Seneca wrote On Anger for his brother Novatus. He treats anger like a trial: no court would convict on hearsay, yet we condemn friends on the strength of a rumor.

text: It was the custom of Sextius when the day was over, and he had betaken himself to rest, to inquire of his spirit: “What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?” Anger will cease, and become more gentle, if it knows that every day it will have to appear before the judgment seat.
author: Seneca
question: Looking back over today, where did you act well, and what would you do differently tomorrow?
context: One of the earliest descriptions of a nightly self-review, practiced by the Roman philosopher Quintus Sextius. Seneca goes on to say he does it himself every night, once the lamp is taken away.

text: I am not a wise man, and I will not be one in order to feed your spite: so do not require me to be on a level with the best of men, but merely to be better than the worst: I am satisfied, if every day I take away something from my vices and correct my faults. I have not arrived at perfect soundness of mind, indeed, I never shall arrive at it: I compound palliatives rather than remedies for my gout, and am satisfied if it comes at rarer intervals and does not shoot so painfully.
author: Seneca
question: What one fault could you make a little smaller today, without demanding perfection of yourself?
context: Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome, and critics called him a hypocrite for preaching simplicity. His answer: he is not a sage, only someone trying to be a little better each day.

text: But what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself? He follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome companionship. We must understand, therefore, that what we suffer from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves: we are weak when there is anything to be endured, and cannot support either labour or pleasure, either one’s own business or any one else’s for long.
author: Seneca
question: What are you hoping a new place, job, or routine will fix that you would carry with you anyway?
context: Written to Seneca's friend Serenus, who complained of restlessness. Just before this, Seneca describes people touring coast after coast to cure their boredom: travel changes the scenery, not the traveler.

text: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry out the most important projects: we have an ample portion, if we do but arrange the whole of it aright: but when it all runs to waste through luxury and carelessness, when it is not devoted to any good purpose, then at the last we are forced to feel that it is all over, although we never noticed how it glided away. Thus it is: we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one, and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them.
author: Seneca
reference: Of the Shortness of Life, I
question: Where did your time go this week that you would not choose to spend it again?
context: The opening argument of On the Shortness of Life, addressed to Paulinus, a Roman official. Seneca's claim is that the problem is not how long life is, but how carelessly we spend it.

text: This chief of yours, whoever he is, though he may look at you in an offensive manner, still will some day look at you, open his ears to your words, and give you a seat by his side: but you never design to look upon yourself, to listen to your own grievances. You ought not, then, to claim these services from another, especially since while you yourself were doing so, you did not wish for an interview with another man, but were not able to obtain one with yourself.
author: Seneca
reference: Of the Shortness of Life, II
question: When did you last give yourself the attention you keep hoping others will give you?
context: Seneca mocks men who resent being kept waiting by powerful patrons while never granting an audience to themselves. "Design" is an older spelling of "deign".

text: You will hear many men say, “After my fiftieth year I will give myself up to leisure: my sixtieth shall be my last year of public office”: and what guarantee have you that your life will last any longer? who will let all this go on just as you have arranged it? are you not ashamed to reserve only the leavings of your life for yourself, and appoint for the enjoyment of your own right mind only that time which you cannot devote to any business? How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it!
author: Seneca
reference: Of the Shortness of Life, III
question: What are you saving for "someday" that belongs in your life now?
context: For Romans, leisure (otium) meant time for study and reflection, not idleness. Seneca attacks the habit of postponing it to retirement, an age many never reach.

text: No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge. Other arts have many folk everywhere who profess to teach them: some of them can be so thoroughly learned by mere boys, that they are able to teach them to others: but one’s whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one’s whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
author: Seneca
reference: Of the Shortness of Life, VII
question: If living well takes a lifetime to learn, what did today give you to practise?
context: "Business man" translates the Latin occupatus, someone who is always busy. Seneca contrasts crafts a boy can master with the art of living, which is never finished.

text: Varro, that most learned of all the Romans, thought that for the mere change of place, apart from the other evils attendant on exile, we may find a sufficient remedy in the thought that wherever we go we always have the same Nature to deal with. Marcus Brutus thought that there was sufficient comfort in the thought that those who go into exile are permitted to carry their virtues thither with them. Though one might think that neither of these alone were able to console an exile, yet it must be confessed that when combined they have great power: for how very little it is that we lose! whithersoever we betake ourselves two most excellent things will accompany us, namely, a common Nature and our own especial virtue.
author: Seneca
question: If you lost your usual place, role, or routine tomorrow, what of real value would still go with you?
context: Seneca wrote this from exile on Corsica to console his mother, Helvia. Instead of asking for pity, he argues that exile takes very little: the natural world and one's own character go everywhere.
